questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a blocking power works
questions.learningObjective: Explain how a permanent member's negative vote defeats a substantive resolution.
questions.stem: Reading the council table, a student must explain why a permanent member's negative vote can stop a substantive resolution.

answer.exemplar: A permanent member's vote against a substantive draft is decisive: the draft fails whatever the numbers in favour. An abstention does not block, because a state that abstains is treated as neither supporting nor opposing. The block also applies only to substantive decisions, so procedural matters and the election of members can still carry by a simple majority.

questions.explanation: The voting column shows a negative vote from a permanent member is decisive on substantive drafts, while an abstention is not a block. That is why a blocking power can freeze the council's real business without leaving it idle.
questions.hint: Contrast a negative vote with an abstention.

options.misconception: believes the assembly makes the threat determination

options.text: The secretary-general must certify that the peace is threatened before the council may act.
options.misconception: assumes the secretary-general decides threats to peace

options.text: The council must itself determine that the situation is a threat, a breach, or an act of aggression.

questions.explanation: The charter summary puts the determination with the council, which must decide whether a situation is a threat, a breach or an act of aggression before other measures follow. The assembly makes no such finding.

questions.topic: How the design entrenched the division
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the council's voting rule froze the wartime division inside the new organisation.

questions.stem: In the table of charter rules, one entry states why the design entrenched the division between the two emerging superpowers; which is that entry?

options.text: The general assembly gave each state one vote, so the more numerous group could outvote the two.
options.misconception: reads assembly equality as the source of the deadlock

options.text: The founding text created a general assembly in which every member could introduce any question.
options.misconception: believes assembly powers caused the split

options.text: Security decisions needed the agreement of the permanent members, including the two on opposite sides.
The council was forbidden from discussing any dispute between a permanent member and another state.
options.misconception: thinks an absolute ban on disputes existed

questions.explanation: Binding council decisions needed the permanent members' agreement, and two of the five sat on opposite sides, so the rules froze the sharpest rivalries inside the design. That is how the division was entrenched.

questions.learningObjective: Explain how a membership body allowed a regional conflict to proceed without a direct clash.
questions.stem: One table row describes a proxy conflict organised through a membership body; explain how the arrangement shielded the two leading camps from each other.

answer.exemplar: The membership body was the forum in which the conflict was handled: its members voted on a response and then supplied troops, money or a command, while the opposing camp supplied neither. Because the decision came from a body that both sides had joined, neither could fairly call it an act of aggression, and the direct clash between the great powers was avoided. Costs and risks were spread across many members instead of falling on two capitals.

questions.explanation: The row shows the conflict managed through a body both camps had entered, with members voting and contributing forces, which let a regional war proceed without the leading powers meeting in open conflict.
questions.hint: Think about decisions taken by member states together.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the design entrenched the division
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a rule about voting entrenched the division it was meant to manage.
questions.stem: The design column of the table shows how the design entrenched the division; explain why the rule on council voting had that effect.

answer.exemplar: The five permanent seats were permanent in two senses: their holders could not be voted out, and each could stop substantive decisions outright. Because two of the five belonged to opposing sides, neither could be outvoted on the matters its rival cared about most. A rule that looked like simple majority government therefore guaranteed that the sharpest disputes could never be settled against a great power, and the division survived inside the constitution of the organisation itself.

questions.explanation: The seats were unremovable and each holder could block, so no side could be outvoted on its vital interests. The rule made the division permanent without ever naming it.
questions.hint: Focus on what the permanent seats and the block combined to do.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The permanent seats created in 1945
questions.learningObjective: Determine how the founding permanent membership related to the wartime alliance.
questions.stem: Given the seat counts in the table, how many of the permanent members had fought on the same side in the war that created the organisation?

answer.exemplar: All five. Every permanent member came from the victorious wartime alliance, so the divisions that soon split the council cannot be explained by the founding membership itself. The seating reflected who had won the war; the paralysis that followed reflected what happened afterwards, when the alliance of yesterday became the rivalry of tomorrow. Reading the two periods together explains why the design looked unremarkable in 1945 and proved so effective at protecting both sides from losing.

questions.explanation: The membership column shows all five permanent members came from the winning wartime alliance, so the later division cannot be read back into the founding membership. It grew from what happened after 1945.
questions.hint: Count the members in the founding column.

questions.topic: The order in which a frozen council was bypassed
questions.learningObjective: Explain why the assembly cannot simply replace a frozen council.
questions.stem: The bypass table shows that the order of steps matters; explain why the general assembly cannot simply take over the council's work.

answer.exemplar: The council was given the authority and the machinery for binding decisions, and the assembly's own resolutions are recommendations rather than commands. When the council is frozen by a veto, the assembly route produces a majority that the party which blocked the council may ignore. The order matters because the assembly step is a pressure device and a demonstration that the blocking power stands isolated, not a substitute for an order that binds. That is why the sequence runs from the council towards the assembly and never the other way round.

questions.explanation: Only the council could order binding measures, so the assembly's vote carries persuasion rather than command. The bypass works as pressure, which is why the council must be tried first.
questions.hint: Compare binding orders with recommendations.

questions.topic: The founding text on threats to the peace
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a determination must precede action on a threat to the peace.
questions.stem: The article notes that a determination of a threat to the peace must precede action; explain the reasoning behind that sequence.

answer.exemplar: The order guarantees that the council, and not the party to the dispute, decides whether the situation is grave enough to justify collective measures. If a state could act first and ask the council to bless it afterwards, the finding would be a formality and the strongest party would set the terms of any settlement. Requiring the determination first also gives later collective action, and any sanction that followed, a shared legal footing rather than the appearance of an act of one state against another.

questions.explanation: The sequence keeps the judgment about seriousness with the body of all members instead of the complainant, and it gives later measures a legal footing. Action first would make the finding a rubber stamp.

answer.exemplar: An economic council let the leader state channel resources to allies on terms it controlled, so a partner's industry, trade and credit stayed inside the bloc rather than moving towards the rival. questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the bargain was accepted
questions.learningObjective: Explain how assembly equality compensated smaller states after a council defeat.
questions.stem: The route table begins with a proposal submitted to the council, followed by a vote that fails; explain how the assembly clause compensated small states for that defeat.

answer.exemplar: The bargain gave small states a forum where they could outvote the great powers, so a proposal defeated in the council could still be carried by an overwhelming majority in the assembly and become the accepted position of the membership. The result was not an order that the great powers had to execute, but it changed what counted as legitimate: a majority of states could declare a course right, and a blocking power could no longer present its veto as the verdict of the world. That moral authority was the compensation for real power sitting elsewhere.

questions.explanation: A defeated proposal could still be carried as the accepted position of the membership, so the veto no longer spoke for the world. Equality of votes was the price small states paid for the council's structure.
questions.hint: Think about what a majority verdict could still achieve.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a blocking power works
questions.learningObjective: Explain the effect of the council's duty to act when a permanent member objects.
questions.stem: Consulting the table, the founding text gives the council a duty to act; explain how that duty works when a permanent member disagrees.

answer.exemplar: The duty is to agree on a determination and then on the measures to be taken, and the text provides that the votes required include the concurring votes of the permanent members. A permanent member that disagrees therefore cannot be forced into a decision, but it cannot erase the finding that the others have made. The council records the determination and the decision, and the dissenting member remains bound by the undertaking to accept the council's decisions in accordance with the founding text, which is why objection is a shield rather than a way out.

questions.explanation: A dissent means no binding decision on measures, but the council can still record a finding and a decision, to which the dissenters remain committed. Objection blocks action; it does not release a member from the text.
questions.hint: Separate the finding from the measures that follow it.

questions.topic: A proxy conflict organised through a membership body
questions.learningObjective: Explain why such a conflict was harder to end than a direct war between two states.
questions.stem: A reader of the table asks why a proxy conflict organised through a membership body was harder to end than a bilateral war; explain the constraint.

answer.exemplar: Every participant had entered the organisation as a member and would have to live with the others afterwards, so the conflict had to be managed inside rules binding all of them. A bilateral war could be ended by the two principals alone; here the command arrangements, the finance and the votes all passed through a body in which the losing side still sat. Any settlement had to be acceptable to states whose interests were not the principals' own, and their access to supplies and votes made them powerful spoilers who had to be bought off rather than defeated.

questions.explanation: Because the body bound all participants, including those on the losing side, a settlement had to satisfy states beyond the two principals. That made ending the conflict slower than a straightforward bilateral war.
questions.hint: Think about who had to be satisfied, not just who was fighting.

options.text: That a majority of the council's elected members have already voted to end the session.
options.misconception: invents a vote of elected members

options.text: That the permanent members have each been invited to attend the assembly's special session.
options.misconception: invites permanent members individually

questions.explanation: The assembly route exists for the case where the body with binding power cannot act, so the council's failure is the precondition for it. A certification or invitation from the permanent members is not required.
questions.hint: The other organ's power depends on this body's power.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the design entrenched the division
questions.learningObjective: Explain how the design kept the organisation together despite constant vetoes.
questions.stem: The veto table's example row shows that a blocking power can refuse an order it dislikes; explain how the design nonetheless kept the organisation together.

answer.exemplar: Two safeguards did the work. The council could still act on everything that did not require the blocked power's agreement, so the organisation never stopped functioning even when the hardest questions were frozen. And the general assembly, where every state held one vote, gave members a place where a blocking power could be outvoted on the question of principle. The veto therefore shaped decisions without making them impossible, which kept both sides inside one framework rather than splitting the organisation into two.

questions.explanation: Much of the council's work continued without the blocked member, and the assembly could outvote it on principle. The design channelled the conflict instead of suspending the organisation.
questions.hint: Think about what still worked when a decision was refused.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: Why the bargain was accepted
questions.learningObjective: Identify what smaller states received in exchange for the permanent seats.

stimulus.body: A note beside the founding table records that five states received seats that could not be voted away, that the remaining council seats were filled at intervals by states chosen by the assembly, and that every member of the organisation had one vote in the assembly itself, where questions of peace were debated at the request of any member.

questions.stem: The table on the founding seat lists five states with unremovable seats; which entry records what smaller states received in the same bargain?

options.text: The right to demand an emergency session of the assembly whenever a permanent member vetoed a draft.
options.misconception: claims smaller states gained a veto of their own

options.text: A seat on the council that could be held without limit for as long as the state wished.
options.misconception: invents an unlimited term for elected seats

options.text: One vote each in the assembly, where decisions were taken by a simple majority of states.
The right to inspect every decision taken by the council before it was published.
options.misconception: invents a veto over publication

questions.explanation: The note pairs the unremovable seats with equality of votes in the assembly, which is the exchange the smaller states accepted. Their influence rested on numbers, and on being able to call debates.
questions.hint: Look for the entry that pairs with the five seats.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The order in which a frozen council was bypassed
questions.learningObjective: Count the formal steps in the bypass sequence accurately.

stimulus.body: An escalation summary records that when the council cannot act, a member may ask for an emergency special session of the assembly, that the request must be made within a short period measured in hours, and that the assembly may then debate the dispute and vote on a recommendation which member states may cite in support of measures of their own.

questions.stem: Counting from the table, the number of steps between a council defeat and an assembly recommendation is what?

options.text: One, because the assembly takes the same draft without a further formal step.
options.misconception: ignores the request for a session

options.text: Three, because the request must also be certified by the chair before the session.
options.misconception: invents a certification stage

options.text: Four, because each permanent member must be notified before a session may convene.
options.misconception: invents a notification requirement

options.text: Two: the request for an emergency session, then the assembly's debate and vote.

questions.explanation: The summary lists the request and then the debate and vote, which are two formal steps after the defeat. It also shows why the request matters: it is what allows the session to be called at short notice.
questions.hint: Count only the steps the summary actually lists.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: A proxy conflict organised through a membership body
questions.learningObjective: Identify how a campaign under a membership body's authority typically ended.
questions.stem: The vote taken by a membership body's council decided that the fighting must stop; what typically followed in such campaigns?

options.text: A permanent member assumed sole command of the forces that had been fighting.
options.misconception: claims one member took over command at the end

options.text: The organisation withdrew and left the two sides to settle the dispute alone.
options.misconception: describes a withdrawal the body never made

options.text: Member contingents withdrew and the body took on the task of keeping the peace.
The fighting continued under a different name until a later council session ended it.
options.misconception: claims the fighting simply changed form

questions.explanation: In campaigns run under the body's authority, the units were withdrawn and the body itself took responsibility for policing the outcome. That transfer of responsibility was the mark of a managed settlement.
questions.hint: Compare what happened to the contingents and to the body itself.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The features of a bloc built against another
questions.learningObjective: Identify the function of the economic grouping attached to each bloc.
questions.stem: The bloc-features table records that the economic grouping on each side existed to do what?

options.text: Channel the leader's resources to allies so that trade and credit stayed inside the bloc.
Fix the price of every traded good so that members could not undercut one another.
options.misconception: invents a bloc-wide price control

options.text: Give members a common currency so that payments between them would need no agreement.
options.misconception: claims a common currency was created

options.text: Set aside the leader's own trade rules so that allies could compete on equal terms.
options.misconception: reverses the reality of the arrangement

questions.explanation: The economic grouping was a channel for resources and a way of keeping allied trade inside the group under the leader's terms. Currency, prices and free competition played no part in it.
questions.hint: Think about where the leader's money and markets went.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The permanent seats created in 1945
questions.learningObjective: Explain how smaller states could still expect representation on the council.
questions.stem: The bargain table's last row records that small states accepted permanent seats for five states; explain how they could still expect their own representation.

answer.exemplar: Elected seats answered that question. The permanent members held five of the council's fifteen places, and the remaining ten were filled at intervals by states elected by the assembly, with rules spread across regions to keep the elected membership rotating. Small states also gained a guaranteed voice in the assembly itself, where every delegation had one vote and where any member could call for a debate. Representation was therefore preserved in numbers, even though decisions on the sharpest disputes rested with five.

questions.explanation: Ten of the fifteen council seats were filled by election, and the assembly gave every state a vote and the right to speak. Small states kept representation even where decisions were made by five.
questions.hint: Count the seats that were not permanent.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How a blocking power works
questions.learningObjective: Explain why a blocking power cannot retire a proposal for good.

stimulus.body: A voting note records that a draft defeated by a negative vote may be revised and submitted again, that a revised draft is voted on as a new proposal, and that the practice of pressing the same question at the next session continued for as long as the members wished to pursue it.

questions.stem: The voting note records that a blocked draft fails; what does the possibility of resubmission reveal about the block?

options.text: That the block is permanent once exercised, since the draft cannot return.
options.misconception: believes the block is final and permanent

options.text: That the block applies only to the wording used, so any new wording escapes it.
options.misconception: assumes any rewording would pass

options.text: That the blocking power is checked by rules that prevent a permanent member from voting twice.
options.misconception: invents a rule against voting twice

options.text: That it is a delay rather than a defeat, since a later vote may meet the same rules.

questions.explanation: Because a revised draft may be tabled again, the block postpones rather than concludes. That keeps the pressure on the blocking power, which is the point of the practice.
questions.hint: Think about what happens to a proposal after a failed vote.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: The founding text on threats to the peace
questions.learningObjective: Explain the purpose of the condition attached to self-defence.

stimulus.body: A clause in the founding text preserves the right of a state to defend itself if an armed attack occurs against it, and states that this right continues only until the council has taken measures which the parties agree to restore international peace. The clause further requires that any measures taken in self-defence be no wider than the demands of the defence.

questions.stem: The escalation column's closing entry shows that a vetoed proposal can still become an assembly recommendation; on threats to the peace, what does the self-defence condition protect?

options.text: It prevents a state from using self-defence as a cover for continuing a war of its own choosing.
It allows a state to keep fighting until the council has finished debating the dispute.
options.misconception: misreads the time limit on self-defence

options.text: It removes the need for the council to take any measure at all in a self-defence case.
options.misconception: claims the council need never act

options.text: It lets a state refuse the council's measures while its own defensive action continues.
options.misconception: invents a right to refuse measures

questions.explanation: The condition ties the right to a specific injury and to the shortest response needed to meet it, and it ends when the council acts. Together these stop a war of choice from being dressed up as defence.
questions.hint: Ask what the limits on scope and duration are for.

questions.subject: WORLD_HISTORY
questions.topic: How the design entrenched the division
questions.learningObjective: Synthesise why the founding design gave the division a durable institutional form.
questions.stem: The charter summary closes by reminding readers that decisions on peace are the council's alone; in the design column, the division was entrenched because what?

options.text: The assembly was barred from discussing any dispute that concerned a permanent member.
options.misconception: invents a bar on assembly discussion

options.text: The permanent members were chosen mainly for their colonial holdings rather than their power.
options.misconception: gives colonial holdings as the selection basis

options.text: The body that could order action contained permanent seats for both sides of the conflict.
The rules required every dispute to be settled by arbitration before the council was consulted.
options.misconception: claims arbitration had to come first

questions.explanation: Because binding authority sat with a body whose permanent members came from both camps, each side could protect itself and its allies. The division was given a durable institutional form rather than merely reflected in politics.
questions.hint: Look at the composition of the body that decides.
